readingInstruction: Read Psalm 119:97-144. This section is the heart of the psalm. Notice how the psalmist describes the sweetness, the light, and the righteousness of God’s word.
settingTheScene: This is the third reading from Psalm 119, covering stanzas thirteen through eighteen. It contains the famous verse 105, the lamp, and some of the strongest statements about how God’s word gives wisdom. It fits the theme of the unit: the commandments as a source of insight and a guide for life.
observation: “Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day” (v. 97).
“Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me” (v. 98).
“I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation” (v. 99).
“How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (v. 103).
“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (v. 105).
“The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple” (v. 130).
“My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law” (v. 136).
“Your testimonies are righteous forever; give me understanding that I may live” (v. 144).
interpretation:
The stanza that begins at verse 97 starts with an exclamation: “Oh how I love your law!” The psalmist does not just obey. He loves. His meditation is constant, “all the day.” This is the Bible’s picture of a believer who treasures God’s word as a delight and a source of wisdom.

The claims of verses 98 to 100 are striking. The psalmist says he is wiser than his enemies, his teachers, and the aged. This is not arrogance but a statement about the power of the word. A humble student of Scripture may have more insight than a clever person who ignores it. Wisdom is not a matter of age or education. It is a matter of heeding God’s testimonies.

Verse 103 describes the word as sweet: “sweeter than honey.” It is both nourishing and delightful. And verse 105 gives the great image of the lamp. Verse 130 adds that “the unfolding of your words gives light.” The word brings understanding, especially to the simple. You do not need to be an expert. The unfolding, the opening up, of the word gives light.

The psalm is not naive. The section includes pain. In verse 136, the psalmist’s eyes shed streams of tears because others do not keep the law. Love for God’s word includes grief at its neglect. And in verses 107 and 139, he describes his affliction and his zeal consuming him. This is a person who feels deeply.

Verse 144 closes the passage with a request that sums up what the psalm is about: “Give me understanding that I may live.” Understanding and life belong together. To know God’s word is to live. The psalmist’s prayer is the same as ours: help me to see.
connection: Jesus said, “Man shall not live by bread alone” (Matthew 4:4), and “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63). He grieved over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41), echoing verse 136. Revelation 10:9-10 uses the image of the word as sweet as honey. Paul writes that the Scriptures “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15).
application:
Read a short passage of Scripture today and ask: what is sweet in this?

Pray that you would grieve what grieves God.

Ask for understanding not just to know but to live.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you love about his law.
Ask him for understanding that gives light.
Grieve with him over those who do not keep his law.
